catalog_quote: First of all, the high central vowel /ɨ/ is distinct from the other vowels with respect to stress placement. The following stress placement rules are applied in order until the structural description of one of the rules is satisfied and (primary) stress is assigned to a syllable of the unit in question. S Rule 1: The first non-high-central vocoid preceding the last phonetic syllable of the last polysyllabic morpheme or series of two or more monosyllabic suffixes in the word is stressed. audit.reasoning: The record rests on the only reference grammar of the language (Bruce 1984, PL C-81), held held by the project, with the deciding quotation confirmed verbatim at pp. 62 and 64 and the supporting statements at p. 70 and p. 301 n. 40. The classification (quality/weight-sensitive: [ɨ]-peaked syllables skipped, right-oriented unbounded search from the domain penult, default initial via S3; secondary stress unanalysed) is a faithful reading of Bruce's ordered S Rules 1-3. The 1979 ANU thesis, downloaded now, gives the same rules (pp. 97-98) and confirms. sources.quote: First of all, the high central vowel /ɨ/ is distinct from the other vowels with respect to stress-placement which we will now consider. Stress placement is determined by phonetic syllables (whether or not they are present in underlying forms). The following stress placement rules are applied in order until the structural description of one of the rules is satisfied and (primary) stress is assigned to a syllable of the unit in question. S Rule 1: The first non-high-central vocoid preceding the last phonetic syllable of the last polysyllabic morpheme in the word is stressed. (A [ɨ] preceding a person-number-gender marker is counted as the peak of the last syllable of the preceding morpheme). S Rule 2: The only non-high-central vocoid in the word is stressed. S Rule 3: The first vocoid of the word is stressed. sources.note: The catalog entry is built from the 1984 published grammar (PL C-81, sect. 2.3.1 pp. 62-64, note 40 p. 301); the 1979 thesis gives the same three ordered rules in nearly the same wording and the identical secondary-stress footnote. Differences: the thesis S Rule 1 lacks the 1984 clause about 'a series of two or more monosyllabic suffixes' (only the PNG-marker parenthetical); the rule domain is stated as 'the last polysyllabic morpheme in the word'. sources.note: The paper is a syntax/lexicon study of serial verb constructions. It never mentions stress, accent, tone or syllable weight; the only prosodic remarks are that serial root constructions form single phonological words while juxtaposed clause sequences carry rising non-final intonation and may be separated by pause (p. 23), and that lexicalised roots 'follow the same morphological and phonological rules' as verb roots (p. 33).
